rows.what the ink shows: A compact word is covered by dense black retracing. An upright remains at the right, but its junction with the overwrite does not securely separate the proposed e, s and t.

The initial tall closed loop of l and the later looped descender of p remain distinct. The connecting e and the end of the abbreviated group, including its proposed stop, are swallowed by the horizontal cancellation.

At the left an open c, low linked e and tall looped l remain visible; at the right there is a detached dot followed by the upright and cross-stroke of t. The intervening baseline letters are crossed through or too faded to confirm.
The deleted line below the inserted bien connu is a thick continuous cancellation with only a few isolated upper and lower protrusions. These remnants do not separate the proposed letters of suivant.

The first short group has a flattened loop and an oblique stroke; the later group retains one upright ascender. The long cancellation covers their joins and the proposed h arch, preventing a secure reading of either group.

The character has two full-height stems joined by a deep rounded bowl, with a short upper-right exit. It matches the tall capital U forms in the preceding line; the neighboring lowercase u in u=Uh is a much shorter baseline bowl.

The complete region shows a slightly curved descending stroke with a connected upper knob and no detached dot. There is no separate numeral head or foot that positively distinguishes 1 from an undotted or joined-dot i; the nearby dotted i therefore does not settle this index.

A hooked initial stroke, a small raised stroke before the middle group, and a final upright with a lower loop remain around the long cancellation. The horizontal strike obscures the bodies needed to distinguish the proposed words, so the phrase cannot be resolved securely.

In the separately cancelled upper insertion, the initial open c-loop, connected low middle humps and the two crossing tips of terminal x remain visible above the short strike. These support the four-letter word ceux.

After the small prefix, E has one raised prime, followed by two equality strokes and a second E with a separate horizontal bar above it. The prefix reduces to a tall curled stroke and a separate small mark, which do not securely distinguish the proposed word car.

The baseline capital E and its single upper-right prime are clear. Above E is a horizontal stroke heavily retraced by an angular dark scribble; the ink does not securely establish whether this remains an intended bar or is a cancelled bar.

The cancellation leaves an initial oval, several low rounded loops in the middle group, and an upright in the final group. Its thick horizontal stroke masks enough letter bodies that the three proposed words cannot be securely resolved.
The capital E is followed by one distinct upright prime at its upper right before the tensor sign. There is no second prime between that stroke and the hat over the tensor.
The B is followed by a parenthesis, E, two distinct short raised strokes, a comma, F and the closing parenthesis. Both primes are separately visible above and to the right of E.

A clear v-shaped letter followed immediately by its dot precedes N and its dot, supporting the abbreviation v. rather than a securely spelled-out voir. The preceding curved and separate horizontal strokes remain unallocated, with their textual or insertion-sign status unresolved; the final compressed group does not securely establish the complete ant.
In the rotated margin formula, the cancelled sign retains a left-pointing angular upper portion and a lower horizontal return. The separate uncancelled equals sign stands immediately to its right.

The erased group has an oval fragment toward its left and a rightward joining stroke. The dense horizontal overstrike and crossing diagonal conceal enough of both bodies that On cannot be established letter by letter.

An initial E-shaped upright with separate short top stroke, a later F stem with upper hook, and the tall d ascender remain visible. Heavy horizontal deletion masks the intervening et, the possible comma, and the lower bodies after d.
A rounded o loop is visible at the left of the cancelled word. The following short uprights and downstroke are crossed by the thick rising deletion stroke, preventing a secure n reading.
